title: Short Stuff: Magnetic Pole Switcheroo
summary: Short Stuff episode on Earth's magnetic field and magnetic pole reversals. The hosts explain the dynamo effect in the molten outer core that generates the field, which shields life from high-energy particles and produces auroras. They discuss how magnetic poles wander (excursions) and sometimes flip, a 2020 Scripps Institution of Oceanography study showing the poles wander about ten degrees a year, and the Laschamp excursion about 42,000 years ago, which coincided with glacier expansion, wind pattern changes, megafauna and Neanderthal disappearance, and a weakened magnetic field. They note that future reversals are hard to predict, that a slow reversal would likely be less catastrophic, and that a weaker field affects satellites, including over the South Atlantic Anomaly. A Cambridge Centre for Risk Studies cost estimate of six to forty-two billion dollars for the US is mentioned. The episode closes with listener-mail-style banter and a sign-off.

segments.title: What Earth's magnetic field is
segments.summary: The field comes from a dynamo effect in the molten outer core around a solid iron-nickel inner core. It shields Earth from high-energy particles and creates auroras.

segments.title: Geographic vs magnetic poles
segments.summary: Geographic poles differ from magnetic poles. Magnetic poles move because the core's flow is uneven, and they wander in excursions and can flip, called polarity reversal.

segments.title: 2020 Scripps study on pole wandering
segments.summary: A 2020 Scripps Institution of Oceanography study using 100,000 years of data found the poles wander about ten degrees a year, about ten times the earlier estimate. The hosts compare the motion to a plinko board.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to the topic.
topics: Stuff You Should Know short stuff

segments.title: Laschamp excursion and its effects
segments.summary: The last flip was the Laschamp excursion about 42,000 years ago, named after a lava flow in France. The poles moved quickly, and the event coincided with glacier expansion, wind changes, megafauna and Neanderthal disappearance. A weakened magnetic field is thought to have contributed, with the reversal a symptom.

segments.title: Predicting future reversals and slow vs fast flips
segments.summary: Scientists cannot predict when the next reversal will occur. The Laschamp was fast and severe, while future reversals are likely to take thousands of years and be less catastrophic. Magnetic striping in seafloor lava was discussed in the plate tectonics episode.

segments.title: Technology impacts and the South Atlantic Anomaly
segments.summary: Satellites and spacecraft have trouble passing through the South Atlantic Anomaly, a weak field area between South America and Africa. A Cambridge Centre for Risk Studies estimate put US economic cost at six to forty-two billion dollars, which the hosts discuss.
